questions.q: Let $A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$ have SVD $A=U\Sigma V^{T}$ with singular values $\sigma_1\ge\cdots\ge\sigma_r>0$. The rank-$k$ truncation $A_k=\sum_{i=1}^{k}\sigma_i u_i v_i^{T}$ minimises $\|A-B\|_F$ over rank-$\le k$ matrices $B$. What is the optimal value of $\|A-B\|_F^{2}$?
questions.explain: Eckart–Young: the optimal Frobenius error is the sum of squared tail singular values, $\sum_{i>k}\sigma_i^{2}$. The operator-2-norm version gives $\sigma_{k+1}$ as the optimum.
questions.hint: The total Frobenius energy of $A$ is $\sum_i \sigma_i^{2}$; the truncation keeps the first $k$ and loses the rest.

questions.q: A $5\times 5$ matrix has singular values $\sigma=(4, 3, 1, 0.5, 0)$. What is the relative Frobenius error $\|A-A_2\|_F^{2}/\|A\|_F^{2}$ when truncating to rank $k=2$?
questions.hint: Square each tail singular value, sum, divide by the sum of all squared singular values.

questions.q: Select every statement that is true of the SVD $A=U\Sigma V^{T}$ of a real $m\times n$ matrix $A$.
choices: The right singular vectors $v_i$ are eigenvectors of $A^{T}A$ with eigenvalue $\sigma_i^{2}$.
The left singular vectors $u_i$ are eigenvectors of $AA^{T}$ with eigenvalue $\sigma_i^{2}$.
The singular values are uniquely determined by $A$ even if $U$ and $V$ are not.
If $A$ is square and invertible, $\sigma_i(A^{-1}) = 1/\sigma_i(A)$ for the same ordering.
questions.explain: $A^{T}A=V\Sigma^{T}\Sigma V^{T}$ and $AA^{T}=U\Sigma\Sigma^{T}U^{T}$ make the first two clear. Singular values are unique (the eigenvalues of $A^{T}A$, square-rooted). The last is wrong because $\sigma_i(A^{-1})$ uses the reverse ordering: the largest singular value of $A^{-1}$ is $1/\sigma_n(A)$, the smallest of $A$.
questions.hint: Square the SVD: $A^{T}A$ and $AA^{T}$ are both PSD and share the spectrum $\sigma_i^{2}$. For the inverse, think which singular value of $A$ corresponds to the largest singular value of $A^{-1}$.

questions.q: PCA is run on a centered $n\times d$ data matrix $\tilde X$ with sample covariance $S=\tfrac{1}{n}\tilde X^{T}\tilde X$. Which is the correct relationship between the singular values $\sigma_j$ of $\tilde X$ and the eigenvalues $\lambda_j$ of $S$?
questions.explain: $S = \tfrac{1}{n}\tilde X^{T}\tilde X = \tfrac{1}{n}V\Sigma^{2}V^{T}$, so the eigenvalues of $S$ are $\sigma_j^{2}/n$. PC$_j$ captures variance $\lambda_j$.
questions.hint: Write $\tilde X = U\Sigma V^{T}$ and substitute into the definition of $S$.

questions.q: Three PCs of a centered data matrix capture variances $\lambda_1=12, \lambda_2=3, \lambda_3=1$ (out of total variance $\sum_j \lambda_j = 18$ across all $d$ features, with the remaining $2$ units in PCs $\ge 4$). What fraction of variance is explained by the first two PCs?
questions.explain: $(\lambda_1+\lambda_2)/\sum_j\lambda_j = 15/18 \approx 0.833$.
questions.hint: Divide the partial sum by the total variance.

questions.q: A student claims: 'The first principal component is the direction along which the projected data has the smallest variance, because PCA minimises reconstruction error.' What is wrong?
choices: PCA actually maximises variance along PC1; the equivalent dual statement is that it minimises reconstruction error along the orthogonal complement.
Nothing is wrong — PCA minimises variance.
PCA only minimises reconstruction error if the data has zero mean.
The first PC is the eigenvector with the smallest eigenvalue, not the largest.
questions.explain: PC1 maximises variance of the projection $\tilde X v$ over unit $v$ — equivalently, it is the unit direction that minimises the residual $\|\tilde X - \tilde X vv^{T}\|_F^{2}$ (the orthogonal-complement reconstruction error). The student inverted the variance statement.
questions.hint: Eckart–Young plus the Pythagorean identity: total variance = projected variance + residual variance.

questions.q: For an unweighted undirected graph with $c$ connected components, the dimension of $\ker L$ equals $c$. A graph has Laplacian spectrum (sorted ascending) $\{0, 0, 0, 0.7, 1.2, 2.4, 3.1\}$. How many connected components does it have?
questions.explain: Multiplicity of the eigenvalue $0$ in $L$ equals the number of connected components. Three zeros ⇒ three components.
questions.hint: Count the zero eigenvalues.

questions.q: Which expression equals $f^{T}Lf$ where $L=D-A$ is the combinatorial Laplacian of an unweighted graph $G$?
questions.explain: The Dirichlet energy: $f^{T}Lf = \sum_i d_i f_i^{2} - \sum_{ij}A_{ij}f_i f_j = \sum_{ij\in E}(f_i-f_j)^{2}$. It is the discrete analogue of $\int\|\nabla f\|^{2}$.
questions.hint: Expand $L=D-A$ and group terms by edges.

questions.q: Select every statement that is true of the symmetric normalised Laplacian $L_{\mathrm{sym}} = I - D^{-1/2}AD^{-1/2}$ for a finite weighted graph $G$ with positive vertex degrees.
choices: Its smallest eigenvalue is $0$ with eigenvector $D^{1/2}\mathbf{1}$.
It has eigenvalue $2$ if and only if $G$ has a bipartite connected component.
It is similar to the random-walk Laplacian $L_{\mathrm{rw}} = I - D^{-1}A$ via $D^{1/2}$.
questions.explain: All four are classical: spectrum $\subseteq [0,2]$ by Gershgorin; $L_{\mathrm{sym}}\,D^{1/2}\mathbf{1}=0$; $\lambda=2$ iff a bipartite component exists; and $L_{\mathrm{sym}} = D^{1/2}L_{\mathrm{rw}}D^{-1/2}$ makes them similar (same spectrum).
questions.hint: Each statement is in the first paragraph of any spectral-graph-theory text — verify them by elementary linear algebra.

questions.q: Order the steps of the Ng–Jordan–Weiss spectral clustering algorithm.
items: Form $L_{\mathrm{sym}} = I - D^{-1/2}AD^{-1/2}$ from the affinity matrix $A$.
Run $k$-means on the rows of $\tilde U$ to assign each vertex to a cluster.
Compute the $k$ eigenvectors $u_1,\dots,u_k$ corresponding to the smallest eigenvalues of $L_{\mathrm{sym}}$.
Row-normalise the matrix $U=[u_1,\dots,u_k]$ to obtain $\tilde U$ with unit-length rows.
questions.explain: Build the normalised Laplacian, extract its bottom $k$ eigenvectors, row-normalise them so each vertex lives on $S^{k-1}$, then $k$-means. The row-normalisation step is what distinguishes Ng–Jordan–Weiss from the earlier Shi–Malik variant.
questions.hint: Build operator → eigenvectors → project to sphere → run $k$-means.

questions.q: Cheeger's inequality for the normalised Laplacian states $\lambda_2/2 \le h(G) \le \sqrt{2\lambda_2}$, where $h(G)$ is the graph conductance. Which conclusion is correct?
choices: A small $\lambda_2$ certifies that no small-conductance cut exists.
A small $\lambda_2$ certifies that a small-conductance cut exists, and the spectral sweep cut achieves it up to a square-root factor.
Cheeger's inequality is tight: $\lambda_2 = h(G)^{2}$ for every graph.
questions.explain: Small $\lambda_2$ ⇒ small $h(G)$ (via the upper bound), and the proof's construction — the spectral sweep cut — explicitly realises a cut with conductance $\le\sqrt{2\lambda_2}$. That's the algorithmic content: an eigenvector gives you an approximate sparsest cut.
questions.hint: The bound $h(G)\le\sqrt{2\lambda_2}$ is constructive: the Fiedler vector's sweep cut achieves it.

questions.q: Which of these is a NP-hard combinatorial problem whose continuous relaxation is precisely the bottom eigenvector problem for $L_{\mathrm{sym}}$?
questions.explain: Shi–Malik (2000) showed: minimise $\mathrm{Ncut}(S,\bar S)$ over partitions $S\subset V$ is NP-hard; relax the discrete volume-weighted indicator $f_i \in \{\sqrt{\operatorname{vol}(\bar S)/\operatorname{vol}(S)}, -\sqrt{\operatorname{vol}(S)/\operatorname{vol}(\bar S)}\}$ to any real vector orthogonal to $D^{1/2}\mathbf{1}$, and the optimum is exactly $\lambda_2(L_{\mathrm{sym}})$ achieved by the Fiedler vector. (The simpler $\pm 1$ relaxation is the RatioCut + unnormalised $L$ story.)
questions.hint: The combinatorial-to-continuous bridge in spectral clustering.

questions.q: What role does the damping factor $\alpha\in(0,1)$ play in the PageRank construction $G_\alpha = \alpha P + (1-\alpha)\tfrac{1}{n}\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^{T}$?
choices: It is the eigenvalue of $G_\alpha$ corresponding to the PageRank vector.
It is the rate at which the random surfer follows a link rather than teleporting; the teleportation $(1-\alpha)\tfrac{1}{n}\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^{T}$ guarantees irreducibility.
It is the smallest eigenvalue of $G_\alpha$, and controls the spectral gap.
It is the convergence tolerance of power iteration.
questions.explain: With probability $\alpha$ the surfer follows the link transition $P$; with probability $1-\alpha$ it jumps to a uniformly random page. The rank-one teleportation term guarantees the perturbed chain is irreducible and aperiodic, so Perron–Frobenius gives a unique positive stationary vector. The dominant eigenvalue of $G_\alpha$ is $1$, not $\alpha$.
questions.hint: $\alpha$ controls a probabilistic mixture of two transitions; teleportation is what guarantees the Markov chain is well-behaved.

questions.q: Power iteration on $G_\alpha$ converges geometrically with rate (at most) $\alpha$. For $\alpha=0.85$, roughly how many iterations are needed to drive the residual below $10^{-6}$ (use $\log_{10}(0.85)\approx -0.0706$)?
questions.explain: $\alpha^{t}\le 10^{-6}$ gives $t\ge 6/0.0706\approx 85$. Independent of $n$ — that's the engineering miracle.
questions.hint: Solve $\alpha^{t}=10^{-6}$ for $t$ in log base 10.

questions.q: A student claims: 'PageRank works on any directed graph because $P$ alone is column-stochastic — the damping is just a convenience.' What is wrong?
choices: Without damping, $P$ may have multiple stationary distributions if the chain is reducible (e.g. dangling pages or rank sinks), so the PageRank vector is not well-defined.
$P$ has eigenvalues $> 1$ if the graph has cycles.
questions.explain: Real web graphs have dangling nodes (pages with no outlinks) and rank sinks (groups that link only inwards). Without the teleportation, $P$ is reducible and Perron–Frobenius doesn't give uniqueness. Damping $(1-\alpha)\tfrac{1}{n}\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^{T}$ is what makes the stationary distribution exist, be unique, and be approximable by power iteration.
questions.hint: What goes wrong on a graph with a dangling node?

questions.q: The Johnson–Lindenstrauss lemma says that any $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^{d}$ can be embedded in $\mathbb{R}^{k}$ via a random Gaussian projection with all pairwise distances preserved to factor $1\pm\varepsilon$, provided $k$ satisfies which bound?
questions.explain: JL: $k\ge 8\log n/\varepsilon^{2}$ suffices (with probability $\ge 1-1/n$). The target dimension is independent of the source dimension $d$ — only the number of points and the desired distortion matter.
questions.hint: Union-bound over $\binom{n}{2}$ pairs.

questions.q: How many target dimensions $k$ does JL recommend for $n=10^{4}$ points to be preserved at $\varepsilon=0.1$ distortion (use $\log n \approx 9.21$ for natural log)?
questions.explain: $k\ge 8\ln n/\varepsilon^{2} \approx 8\cdot 9.21 / 0.01 \approx 7368$. The constant in front is sometimes given as $4$ or $24$ depending on the proof; the scaling $\log n/\varepsilon^{2}$ is what matters.
questions.hint: Plug into $k = 8\log n/\varepsilon^{2}$ with $\log=\ln$.

questions.q: Order the steps of randomized SVD (Halko–Martinsson–Tropp) for finding the top-$k$ singular vectors of $A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$.
items: Compute the small SVD $\hat U\hat\Sigma V^{T} = Q^{T}A$ and set $U = Q\hat U$.
Orthonormalise the columns of $Y$ via QR: $Y = QR$.
Draw a random Gaussian sketch matrix $\Omega\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times (k+p)}$.
questions.explain: Sketch → multiply → orthonormalise → restrict-and-decompose. The expensive step is the $A\Omega$ product; everything after that is $O((m+n)(k+p)^{2})$ at most, dwarfed by the sketch.
questions.hint: The flow is: pick a random subspace, project $A$ onto it, decompose the projection.

questions.q: The Nyström approximation $\tilde K = K_{nm}K_{mm}^{+}K_{nm}^{T}$ replaces an $n\times n$ kernel matrix $K$ with a rank-$m$ approximation based on $m$ landmarks. What is the dominant storage cost?
questions.explain: $K_{nm}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times m}$ dominates: $O(nm)$. $K_{mm}^{+}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times m}$ is $O(m^{2})$, negligible when $m\ll n$. The point of Nyström is exactly that you avoid materialising the full $n^{2}$ matrix.
questions.hint: Which of the two blocks is bigger when $m\ll n$?

questions.q: Select every property that the Nyström approximation $\tilde K = K_{nm}K_{mm}^{+}K_{nm}^{T}$ shares with the original positive semidefinite kernel matrix $K$.
choices: Rank: $\tilde K$ has the same rank as $K$.
Eigenvectors: the top-$m$ Nyström eigenvectors are the Nyström extensions of the eigenvectors of $K_{mm}$ to the full point set.
questions.explain: $\tilde K$ is symmetric PSD by construction (a Gram product) and its top-$m$ eigenpairs are the Nyström extensions described. Rank is generally not preserved — $\tilde K$ has rank $\le m$, while $K$ may be full rank.
questions.hint: $\tilde K$ factors as $X^{T}X$ for an explicit $X$; the rank claim conflates 'approximate' with 'exact'.

questions.q: Which landmark-selection scheme provides the strongest theoretical guarantee — needing only $m = O(k\log k/\varepsilon^{2})$ landmarks for relative-$\varepsilon$ recovery of the top-$k$ eigenpairs of a kernel matrix?
choices: $k$-means clustering of the points, then take cluster centers as landmarks.
Leverage-score sampling — sample each point with probability proportional to its diagonal in the projection onto the top-$k$ subspace.
Greedy max-min coverage of the data.
questions.explain: Drineas–Mahoney (2005) and Alaoui–Mahoney (2015): leverage scores are the diagonal entries of $UU^{T}$ where $U$ holds the top-$k$ eigenvectors of $K$. Sampling proportionally to leverage scores beats uniform sampling by a factor of $k$ in the required landmark count, with relative-error guarantees.
questions.hint: The 'importance' of a point for the top-$k$ subspace is encoded in its leverage score.
